statement: In children and adolescents with ADHD taking part in blinded placebo-controlled trials (a meta-analysis of 35 trials searched to August 2017; 3079 on methylphenidate, 2606 on placebo), methylphenidate compared with placebo is associated with sleep problems being recorded more often: insomnia 1.6 times as often (relative risk 1.61; 95% CI 1.45 to 1.78 by the editors' calculation from the reported z), trouble falling asleep 2.8 times (2.78; 2.05 to 3.77), at least one of several types of insomnia 3.0 times (2.97; 2.13 to 4.15) and 'sleep disorder' 2.0 times (1.99; 1.44 to 2.74). The review does not say how many children per 100 had these problems with either treatment, and shows that the relative risk depends strongly on how often the placebo group reported sleep problems and on who recorded them and whether a rating scale was used; for insomnia, most individual trials' adjusted results did not differ significantly from placebo. The trials were not appraised for bias, and the review was funded by a drug company (Ironshore), two authors worked for its parent company, and the first author reported support from 13 companies. The evidence concerns young people taking the medicine as prescribed in trials; adults and non-prescribed use were not studied. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: Across 35 trials in children and teenagers with ADHD, sleep problems, especially trouble falling asleep, were recorded more often in those taking methylphenidate than in those taking a dummy pill: nearly three times as often for trouble falling asleep. The review does not say how many children out of 100 were affected, and how carefully children were asked made a big difference. It was paid for by a company that makes one of these medicines, and it did not study adults or use without a prescription.
population: Children and adolescents aged 6 to 18 with ADHD in double- or triple-blind randomized placebo-controlled trials of methylphenidate products in clinical settings
exposure: Methylphenidate as given in the trials (immediate- and extended-release products; study conditions in the study card)
outcome: Sleep-related adverse events recorded by spontaneous report (MedDRA terms) or rating scales: insomnia, initial insomnia, middle insomnia, combined insomnia, sleep disorder
magnitude: Pooled relative risks: insomnia 1.61 (z = 9.2), initial insomnia 2.78 (z = 6.6), combined insomnia 2.97 (z = 6.4), sleep disorder 1.99 (z = 4.2), all p < 0.001; middle insomnia 2.97 with an implausible printed z (183). Editors' 95% CIs from RR and z: 1.45 to 1.78; 2.05 to 3.77; 2.13 to 4.15; 1.44 to 2.74. No absolute rates or heterogeneity statistics are reported; drug and placebo adverse-event rates correlated r = 0.89, and more than 75% of individual trials' adjusted relative risks for insomnia did not differ significantly from 1.

evidence.extracted: 35 trials, 75 observations, 3079 patients on methylphenidate and 2606 on placebo; pooled relative risks insomnia 1.61 (z = 9.2), initial insomnia 2.78 (z = 6.6), middle insomnia 2.97 (z printed as 183), combined insomnia 2.97 (z = 6.4), sleep disorder 1.99 (z = 4.2), all p < 0.001.

evidence.page: Results › Meta-Analysis of Odds Ratios Adjusted for Confounders; Figure 2
evidence.locator: Results › Meta-Analysis of Odds Ratios Adjusted for Confounders, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 legend
evidence.extracted: Adjusted relative risks for insomnia in individual trials ranged widely: more than 75% not significantly different from 1, some significantly below 1 and some above 1; Egger's test t = 0.37, p = 0.7.

evidence.page: Results › The Impact of Placebo AE Rates on the RR Statistic; Discussion
evidence.locator: Results › The Impact of Placebo AE Rates on the RR Statistic; Discussion, 8th and 9th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Drug and placebo adverse-event rates were highly correlated (r = 0.89, p < 0.0001) and observed relative risks were close to those predicted from the placebo rate alone; citing Wernicke et al., the authors note that eliciting adverse events gives higher absolute rates in both groups, while spontaneous reporting more often gives larger relative risks; so relative risks should be read with absolute risks, which the review does not report in its text.

Manuscript development funded by Ironshore Pharmaceuticals & Development, a subsidiary of Highland Therapeutics; two PharmDs from Ironshore assisted with data extraction and two authors are employees of Highland Therapeutics; the first author reported income or support from 13 companies, including Ironshore.

risk_of_bias.note: Trials not appraised by the review; varied ways of recording sleep problems; manufacturer-funded review with employee extractors.

inconsistency.note: Wide spread of individual adjusted relative risks; no I2 or tau2 reported.

indirectness.note: Worded for prescribed use in young people with ADHD; adults and non-prescribed use are named as not studied.

publication_bias.note: Egger's test non-significant, though printed identically for two sets of trials; not downgraded.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high. Risk of bias -1 (the trials were not appraised; adverse-event ascertainment varied; the review has critical flaws under AMSTAR 2 and manufacturer funding). Inconsistency -1 (individual trials' adjusted relative risks fall on both sides of 1, and heterogeneity is not quantified). Not downgraded for imprecision (narrow intervals by the editors' calculation) or indirectness (the claim is worded for young people with ADHD in trials). Low. Status replicated: 35 trials pooled to consistently raised relative risks, although per-trial directions are visible only in figures not read.

statement: In children and adolescents with ADHD (9 small studies with 246 young people, mostly boys, average ages about 8 to 12 years; a meta-analysis searched to March 2015; Kidwell et al., 2015), nights on stimulant medicine (methylphenidate in 6 studies; amphetamine-type medicines, including lisdexamfetamine and mixed amphetamine salts, in 3) compared with nights without it are associated with taking longer to fall asleep (standardized difference 0.78, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.02; 0.54, 0.28 to 0.81, after a correction for possibly missing studies; 7 studies, 171 young people), less efficient sleep (−0.39, −0.69 to −0.08; −0.32 after correction; 7 studies) and shorter sleep (−0.59, −0.84 to −0.35; 7 studies, 223 young people), measured with wrist activity monitors or overnight sleep recordings. Differences between studies were large (I² 67% to 83%), and the review gives no results in minutes. Although it included only studies with random assignment, it compared medicated nights mostly with nights before treatment began (placebo nights in 4 studies), converted some results using an assumed correlation, and did not report the trials' risk of bias. Comparing studies with each other, the effect on sleep efficiency was smaller where children had taken the medicine for more days, which does not show that a child's sleep adapts. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In 9 studies of children and teenagers with ADHD who wore sleep monitors, nights on stimulant medicine (methylphenidate or amphetamine-type medicines) were compared with nights without it. On medicine, they took longer to fall asleep, slept less, and their sleep was less efficient. The review does not say by how many minutes. The effect on sleep efficiency looked smaller in studies where children had taken the medicine for longer, but that comparison between studies cannot show that sleep gets better with time.
population: Children and adolescents with ADHD (mean ages about 8.5 to 11.6 years; 42% to 85% boys) in 9 small studies with random assignment to stimulant conditions and actigraphy or polysomnography
exposure: Nights on prescribed stimulant medicine: methylphenidate (6 studies) or amphetamine-class medicines, including lisdexamfetamine and mixed amphetamine salts (3 studies); study conditions in the study card
comparator: The same children's unmedicated nights: mostly pre-treatment baseline nights, placebo nights in 4 studies
outcome: Sleep latency, sleep efficiency and total sleep time measured by actigraphy or polysomnography
magnitude: Hedges' g (random effects): sleep latency 0.78 (95% CI 0.54 to 1.02), I² 67.30%, after trim-and-fill 0.54 (0.28 to 0.81); sleep efficiency −0.39 (−0.69 to −0.08), I² 83.37%, after trim-and-fill −0.32 (−0.63 to −0.01); total sleep time −0.59 (−0.84 to −0.35), I² 82.67%, no asymmetry. No differences in minutes are reported.

evidence.locator: Abstract (p. 1); Methods › Study Selection (p. 2); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 5)
evidence.extracted: Nine studies with 246 young people were included from 9927 records and 167 full texts; eligibility required random assignment to stimulant conditions and actigraphy or polysomnography; studies were collected through March 2015.

evidence.locator: Methods › Data Extraction; Effect Size Calculation
evidence.extracted: Effect sizes compared baseline with medicated sleep, with placebo nights used where a study gave no baseline (4 studies), and a correlation of 0.5 was assumed when the needed statistics were missing.

evidence.locator: Results › The Effect of Stimulant Medications on Sleep Latency, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Sleep latency, 7 samples (N = 171): g = 0.78 (95% CI 0.54 to 1.02), I² 67.30%; after trim-and-fill with 3 imputed studies, 0.54 (0.28 to 0.81).

evidence.locator: Results › The Effect of Stimulant Medications on Sleep Efficiency
evidence.extracted: Sleep efficiency, 7 samples (N = 155): g = −0.39 (−0.69 to −0.08), I² 83.37%; after trim-and-fill with 1 imputed study, −0.32 (−0.63 to −0.01); the negative effect was smaller in studies with more days on medication (b = 0.05 per day).

evidence.locator: Results › The Effect of Stimulant Medications on Total Sleep Time
evidence.extracted: Total sleep time, 7 samples (N = 223): g = −0.59 (−0.84 to −0.35), I² 82.67%, with no funnel-plot asymmetry and no significant moderators.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (read on the rendered, rotated page)
evidence.extracted: Single-study effects: sleep latency 0.44 to 1.15, all longer on medication; sleep efficiency −1.76 to 0.48, one study better on medication; total sleep −1.31 to −0.16, all shorter; mean ages 102 to 139.2 months.

The authors note that publication bias was present for latency and efficiency, that the correction may underestimate effects and that moderator results rest on few studies; there was no external funding.

risk_of_bias.note: The pooled contrasts are mostly medicated against pre-treatment nights rather than the randomized placebo contrast; the trials' risk of bias was not reported; correlations were assumed; two samples may overlap.

inconsistency.note: I² 67% to 83%, but sleep onset and total sleep point the same way in every study, and efficiency in six of seven.

indirectness.note: Worded for prescribed use in young people with ADHD.

imprecision.note: Intervals exclude no effect for all three outcomes.

publication_bias.note: Funnel asymmetry for latency and efficiency (studies imputed by trim-and-fill); published studies only.

grade.reasoning: Studies with random assignment start high, but the pooled contrasts are mostly within-child comparisons with pre-treatment nights. Risk of bias −1 and publication bias −1 give low. Status replicated: every study found longer sleep onset and shorter sleep on medication. This complements the meta-analysis of reported sleep problems in placebo-controlled methylphenidate trials (Faraone et al., 2019), which draws on a partly overlapping literature.

statement: In children aged 6 to 14 with ADHD who were taking stimulant medicine and still took more than an hour to fall asleep (on average, or on at least 30% of nights) after a sleep-routine programme (a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in a Vancouver hospital ADHD programme, 19 children analysed, sponsored by the company that made the melatonin; Weiss et al., 2006), melatonin (study conditions in the study card) compared with placebo is associated with falling asleep about 16 minutes sooner on parents' sleep diaries (46.4 against 62.1 minutes; effect size 0.6) and sooner on wrist activity monitors, and with about 15 minutes more sleep on the diaries but not on the monitors. Clinicians' overall ratings of improvement and parents' ratings of ADHD symptoms did not differ between melatonin and placebo; side effects were mild or moderate and were reported about as often with placebo (20% of all reported side effects during melatonin, 23% during placebo). The trial analysed fewer children than its own power calculation required, its statistics imply more children than the 19 it reports, and children's sleep improved over time whatever they took (a significant period effect). Whether melatonin helps without a sleep routine, in children not taking stimulants, or over months under blinded conditions is not known. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Children with ADHD whose medicine kept them awake took melatonin on some nights and a dummy pill on others, without knowing which. With melatonin they fell asleep about 16 minutes sooner. Doctors did not see a bigger overall improvement with melatonin than with the dummy pill, and side effects were mild and as common with the dummy pill. It was one small study, paid for by the company that made the melatonin.
population: Children aged 6 to 14 (91% boys) with ADHD on stable stimulant medicine whose time to fall asleep stayed over an hour after a sleep-hygiene programme, in a hospital ADHD programme
exposure: Pharmaceutical-grade melatonin made by the sponsor (study conditions in the study card)
comparator: Placebo, in a randomized crossover with each child as his or her own control
outcome: Time to fall asleep and total sleep (parent diaries, actigraphy), clinician-rated improvement, ADHD symptoms, adverse events
magnitude: Diary sleep-onset latency 46.4 (SD 26.4) against 62.1 (SD 26.6) minutes, t(20) = −3.06, p < .01, effect size 0.6; actigraph t(18) = −4.54, p < .01; diary total sleep 15.0 minutes longer, t(20) = 3.13; actigraph total sleep, clinician ratings and ADHD ratings not different; 20% against 23% of all adverse events.

evidence.locator: Method › Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Procedures (p. 514); Results › Patients, 1st paragraph (p. 515)
evidence.extracted: Children aged 6 to 14 on stable stimulant medicine with sleep-onset latency over 60 minutes on parents' diaries; those still above 60 minutes (on average, or on at least 30% of nights) after sleep hygiene were randomized by the pharmacy in blocks of four to melatonin and placebo in a crossover with placebo washouts; of 23 eligible, 1 withdrew and 3 were discontinued for protocol violations, and 19 were analysed per protocol.

evidence.locator: Results › Melatonin Versus Placebo, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Diary sleep-onset latency was 46.4 minutes (SD 26.4) on melatonin and 62.1 (SD 26.6) on placebo, t(20) = −3.06, p < .01, effect size 0.6, with a significant period effect, t(20) = −2.20, and no carryover; actigraph latency was also shorter, t(18) = −4.54, p < .01; diary total sleep was 15.0 minutes longer, t(20) = 3.13.

evidence.locator: Results › Melatonin Versus Placebo, 3rd paragraph; Safety
evidence.extracted: Clinician-rated treatment response and ADHD ratings did not differ between melatonin and placebo; adverse events were mild or moderate except one severe migraine, the only study-related event was a rash from the actigraph band, and twenty per cent of all adverse events occurred during melatonin and 23% during placebo.

evidence.locator: Title page footnote (p. 512); Method › Medication and Statistical Analysis (p. 515); Disclosure (p. 518)
evidence.extracted: Sponsored as an investigator-initiated trial by Circa Dia BV, which manufactured the melatonin; the first author disclosed ties with Circa Dia and several makers of ADHD medicines; the study aimed to detect a 30-minute change with 25 children.

risk_of_bias.note: Per-protocol analysis whose degrees of freedom do not match the stated 19 children; a significant period effect; no registration; the product was made by the sponsor.

inconsistency.note: Single study; diaries and monitors agree in direction.

indirectness.note: Worded for children on stimulants whose insomnia persisted after a sleep-hygiene run-in.

imprecision.note: One trial of about 20 children; no confidence interval for the difference.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for a single trial.

grade.reasoning: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover starts high. Risk of bias −1 and imprecision −1 give low. Status single study.

statement: In children aged 6 to 14 with ADHD who were taking stimulant medicine and took more than an hour to fall asleep (27 or 28 children in the run-in phase of a trial in a Vancouver hospital ADHD programme; Weiss et al., 2006), a sleep-routine programme (a regular bedtime and waking time, no caffeine and no naps, worked out with parents from sleep diaries), compared with the same children's sleep before it, is associated with falling asleep sooner: from 91.7 to 69.3 minutes on parents' diaries and from 98.1 to 73.0 minutes on wrist activity monitors (effect size 0.67), with less variation from night to night on the diaries. Only 5 children then fell asleep within an hour, clinicians rated 21% much or very much improved and 54% unchanged, and ADHD ratings did not change. There was no comparison group, so part of the change may have happened anyway, for example because children were chosen when their sleep was at its worst. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Families of children on ADHD medicine who took over an hour to fall asleep kept a set bedtime and waking time and cut out caffeine and naps. Afterwards the children fell asleep a little over 20 minutes sooner than before, but only 5 of them fell asleep within an hour. There was no comparison group, so some of this change might have happened anyway.
population: Children aged 6 to 14 with ADHD on stable stimulant medicine taking more than 60 minutes to fall asleep, in a hospital ADHD programme
exposure: A sleep-hygiene programme: a consistent bedtime and waking time, no caffeine and no naps, reviewed with parents from sleep diaries (study conditions in the study card)
comparator: The same children's sleep in the nights before the programme (no control group)
outcome: Time to fall asleep (parent diaries and actigraphy), night-to-night variability, clinician-rated improvement, ADHD symptoms
magnitude: Sleep-onset latency 91.7 to 69.3 minutes on diaries (t(28) = 2.77, p = .01) and 98.1 to 73.0 on actigraphy (t(21) = 2.92, p < .01); effect size 0.67; diary variability 47.7 to 29.1 minutes; 5 children below 60 minutes; clinicians: 21% much or very much improved, 54% unchanged.

evidence.locator: Method › Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Procedures › Sleep Hygiene
evidence.extracted: Inclusion required stimulant medicine at an unchanged dose and a mean sleep-onset latency over 60 minutes on 10 nights of parent diaries; sleep hygiene meant reviewing the diaries with parent and child, choosing a consistent bedtime and waking time, and stopping caffeine and naps.

evidence.locator: Results › Response to Sleep Hygiene, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Sleep-onset latency fell from 91.7 to 69.3 minutes on diaries (t(28) = 2.77, p = .01) and from 98.1 to 73.0 on actigraphy (t(21) = 2.92, p < .01), effect size 0.67; diary variability fell from 47.7 to 29.1 minutes; five children met the response criterion (under 1 hour); clinicians rated 21% much or very much improved, 21% minimally improved and 54% unchanged; ADHD ratings did not change.

The abstract gives twenty-seven children receiving sleep hygiene; the participant flow gives 33 consenting, five withdrawing and five responding to sleep hygiene, leaving 23 eligible for randomization; this phase had no control group.

risk_of_bias.note: No control group; children selected for long sleep onset invite regression to the mean; parents knew the programme had begun.

inconsistency.note: Single study; diary and actigraph agree.

indirectness.note: Worded for the children and setting studied.

imprecision.note: About 28 children; the before-after change is precise but its cause is not.

grade.reasoning: An uncontrolled before-after comparison starts low; risk of bias −1 gives very low. Status single study.
